steps: Save an array to a .npy path.
Load it back into a new name.
Print both and confirm the values match.
save and load.realWorld: Caching a prepared array between runs is a save/load pair, and no parsing or dtype guessing is involved.
mistakes: Opening the .npy file in a text editor and expecting numbers.
Forgetting the extension — save appends .npy automatically.
revision: .npy is a binary format that stores dtype and shape.
load restores the array exactly.

steps: Write an integer array to a text file.
Read it back with loadtxt.
Note the values came back as floats.
Text and CSV round-trip.realWorld: When another tool must read the data, a text file is the portable choice even though it loses dtype information.
mistakes: Expecting loadtxt to recover the original integer dtype.
Writing with the default precision and losing digits.
revision: Text files are human- and tool-readable but lossy on dtype.
Pass dtype=int to loadtxt to get integers back.

steps: Save one named array into an npz archive.
Load the archive and print its keys.
Index the archive by the name you gave.
Several arrays in one NPZ.realWorld: Shipping a dataset's features and labels as one file keeps them from being separated or mismatched.
mistakes: Passing arrays positionally, which names them arr_0, arr_1.
Expecting the archive to be compressed; savez does not compress.
revision: savez takes keyword names, which become the keys.
load returns a mapping-like object, not a single array.

steps: Write a CSV with a header row.
Load it with skiprows=1.
Confirm only the numeric rows came through.
skiprows ignores a header line.realWorld: Exported CSVs almost always carry a header, and skiprows is the one argument that keeps loadtxt from failing on it.
mistakes: Forgetting skiprows and getting a parse error on the header.
Assuming skiprows understands column names.
revision: loadtxt has no header concept.
skiprows drops the header before parsing numbers.

steps: Write a CSV with one empty field.
Read it with genfromtxt.
Confirm the gap became nan.
genfromtxt fills missing values.realWorld: Real exports have holes, and genfromtxt keeps the row count intact instead of failing the whole file.
mistakes: Using loadtxt and getting a ValueError on the empty field.
Forgetting to handle the nan before computing a mean.
revision: genfromtxt tolerates gaps and fills nan.
loadtxt requires every field to parse.

steps: Save two arrays under two names.
Print the sorted file keys.
Fetch one array by name and check its values.
npz stores several arrays.realWorld: A model bundle of weights, means and scales travels as one archive with three keys.
mistakes: Iterating the archive instead of its .files list.
Forgetting arrays are only read when indexed.
revision: files lists the stored names.
Indexing by key returns that array.

steps: Write a raw float64 file with tofile.
Map it with an explicit dtype and shape.
Index one element and print it.
memmap reads without loading everything.realWorld: Datasets larger than memory are indexed through a memory map, so only the touched pages are read from disk.
mistakes: Mismatching dtype or shape against the file and reading garbage.
Forgetting raw files carry no dtype or shape metadata.
revision: memmap needs the dtype and shape supplied by you.
It behaves like an array but reads pages on demand.

steps: Write an integer matrix with a comma delimiter.
Set fmt='%d' so no decimals appear.
Print the file contents.
savetxt writes formatted text.realWorld: Feeding a spreadsheet or a legacy importer means writing integers as integers, which fmt controls.
mistakes: Leaving the default fmt and writing 1.000000000000000000e+00.
Choosing a delimiter the reader does not expect.
revision: fmt decides how each value is stringified.
delimiter and fmt must match the consumer's expectations.

steps: Save a small array.
Load it back.
Print the values and confirm they are identical.
Save one array and load it back.realWorld: Intermediate results that must survive a restart are saved, and the dtype comes back with them.
mistakes: Recomputing instead of caching a slow step.
Assuming the file is portable across Python versions without care.
revision: .npy keeps dtype and shape.
load returns the array with no conversion step.

steps: Read a CSV with a header using names=True.
Print the field names.
Index a column by name.
genfromtxt reads named columns.realWorld: Code that refers to a column by name survives a reordered export, which positional indexing does not.
mistakes: Using positional indexing after asking for names.
Forgetting names=True and getting a plain 2-D array.
revision: names=True turns the header into field names.
The result is a structured array indexed by name.

steps: Write a file whose first line starts with #.
Load it with dtype=int.
Confirm the comment vanished and the dtype is integer.
loadtxt skips comment lines.realWorld: Config-style data files carry comments, and loadtxt drops them without any preprocessing.
mistakes: Assuming comments need an explicit flag; '#' is the default.
Leaving dtype float and getting decimals in integer data.
revision: Lines beginning with # are ignored by default.
dtype controls the parsed type.

steps: Save two arrays under two names.
Load the archive and list its keys.
Fetch one array and print its values.
An npz file exposes its arrays by key.realWorld: Discovering what a saved bundle contains before loading it is a keys call, which keeps code from guessing names.
mistakes: Indexing a name that was never saved.
Confusing the archive object with a dict of loaded arrays.
revision: load on an npz returns a mapping-like archive.
Keys are the keyword names used at save time.

steps: Save a float32 array.
Load it back.
Print the values, dtype and shape.
save and load one array.realWorld: Preserving dtype is why .npy beats CSV for a training cache: float32 stays float32 and no rounding happens.
mistakes: Using CSV and silently widening float32 to float64.
Assuming save writes human-readable output.
revision: save keeps dtype and shape exactly.
No text conversion happens in either direction.

steps: Save two differently shaped arrays under names.
List the keys of the archive.
Print the shape of the second one.
savez stores several arrays.realWorld: A pack of features, labels and metadata belongs in one file so the pieces cannot drift apart.
mistakes: Positional arguments producing arr_0 names.
Expecting savez to compress; use savez_compressed for that.
revision: savez groups named arrays into one archive.
load indexes them by the names you chose.

steps: Write a CSV with a text column and a numeric column.
Read it with dtype=None so each column is typed.
Print the field names and sum the numeric column.
genfromtxt types a whole table.realWorld: Mixed tables — names beside numbers — need per-column types, which a single float dtype cannot express.
mistakes: Leaving the default dtype and getting every column as a string.
Forgetting encoding='utf-8' on non-ASCII text.
revision: dtype=None infers a type per column.
The result is a structured array with named fields.

memmap writes through to disk.syntax: m = np.memmap(p, mode='r+', dtype=..., shape=...); m.flush()
steps: Write a raw float64 file.
Map it read-write and assign one cell.
Flush and read the file back with fromfile.
memmap writes through to disk.realWorld: Editing one record of a huge dataset in place is a memmap write, with no full load or rewrite.
mistakes: Forgetting flush and reading a stale file.
Opening mode='r' and trying to assign into it.
revision: mode='r+' makes the map writable.
flush pushes changed pages back to the file.

steps: Save a long range under compression.
Open the archive and list its keys.
Sum the array to confirm the values survived.
savez_compressed shrinks an archive.realWorld: Repetitive arrays compress dramatically, which matters when a dataset has to be uploaded or checked into storage.
mistakes: Using compression for data that is already dense and random.
Expecting the same write speed as savez.
revision: savez_compressed adds deflate compression.
The keyed access is identical to savez.

steps: Write a three-column CSV.
Load only columns 0 and 2.
Confirm the result has two columns in the order asked.
loadtxt with selected columns.realWorld: A wide export with one useful pair of columns loads faster when the rest are never parsed.
mistakes: Expecting usecols to reorder or rename columns.
Passing a column index that does not exist.
revision: usecols selects and orders the parsed columns.
The file's other columns are never converted.

steps: Write a value with four decimals using fmt='%.2f'.
Read the file and print it.
Note the precision was decided at write time.
savetxt with a format string.realWorld: Round-tripping through text loses digits, so the format string is the contract for how much precision survives.
mistakes: Assuming loadtxt recovers the lost digits.
Using a format that truncates an ID or a timestamp.
revision: fmt controls precision in the written file.
Text output is lossy unless the format keeps every digit.

steps: Write a float32 array with tofile.
Read it back with fromfile and the same dtype.
Print the dtype and values.
tofile and fromfile for raw binary.realWorld: Interchange with C, Fortran or a GPU buffer uses raw bytes, where you control the dtype on both ends.
mistakes: Reading with the wrong dtype and getting noise.
Expecting fromfile to restore the shape.
revision: tofile writes the buffer with no header.
fromfile needs the dtype and returns a flat array.

steps: Save an object array.
Try to load it with allow_pickle=False and catch the error.
Load again with allow_pickle=True and read the key.
load refuses pickled objects.realWorld: Loading a file from an untrusted source with pickle enabled can execute code, so numeric arrays should stay numeric.
mistakes: Setting allow_pickle=True by default in a loader.
Storing dicts or strings in an array where a structured dtype would do.
revision: Object arrays require pickle to rebuild.
allow_pickle=False is the safe default for untrusted files.
